metadata.title: The Script, Not The Understanding.
metadata.subtitle: The Workshop Skill (Coaching Script vs. Actual Understanding)
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: does Claude's workshop-coaching skill guarantee the participant actually understands Claude Managed Agents by the end, or only that Claude explains things correctly along the way? Lands the carry-out that a SKILL.md file fixes exactly what Claude says, not whether it lands.

beats.narration_text: Someone assumed Claude's workshop skill would build their SEC agents. Here's what's actually happening: it coaches you through the work, act by act. They optimized for learning, not for shipping. Liam, in for Bear.

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('do' -> 'coach') lands on screen and the full corrected question finishes typing before the clip ends.

beats.narration_text: Here's the machinery. A skill is a folder Claude reads before it acts. This one is a coach for a seven-act SEC-agents training, acts zero through six. The file spells out two modes: you drive while Claude hints, or Claude makes the change and walks you through it after. Either way, it's still one text file, followed act by act — the coaching shape is the same regardless of who's holding the keyboard.

production_viz.label: A SKILL IS A FOLDER
production_viz.caption: One file. Two modes. Same coach.

beats.narration_text: Here's the interesting constraint: when a step breaks, Claude isn't allowed to shortcut. The file explicitly bars reading the solutions folder or the project's git history for the fix. Instead it checks the real documentation and the error message, fixes it forward, and explains what changed — the same explanation you get when the step just works. They optimized for reasoning from the stub at the expense of speed. Stuck or not, the explanation has to come from understanding, never from copying a known answer.

shot.new_visual_element: NO PEEKING AT THE ANSWER KEY

production_viz.label: NO PEEKING AT THE ANSWER KEY
production_viz.caption: Stuck or not: reason it, don't copy it.

beats.narration_text: The file also fixes exactly how each explanation is shaped: what changed, why it works, the platform idea behind it, where to see it live, one thing to try. That's the artifact the SKILL.md can guarantee — Claude's coaching script. Here's what it can't guarantee: whether the participant actually walks away understanding how a managed agent works. That's a different thing entirely, and no text file can promise that part.

production_viz.label: THE SCRIPT, AND THE LEARNING
production_viz.caption: The file reaches the middle step. Not the last one.

beats.narration_text: A SKILL.md file can fix exactly what Claude says next. It can't fix whether the person listening actually understands it.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: Write a short, five-part coaching file — what changed, why it works, the concept it shows, where to see it, one thing to try — for walking someone through fixing an off-by-one bug in a for loop. Follow those exact steps to coach me through one I'll paste in. Then ask me to explain the fix back in my own words, and tell me honestly whether that proves I understood the mechanism, or just that I could repeat the script.

beats.narration_text: Here's a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini — it tests the exact ceiling this SKILL.md hits. Have a model write you a five-part coaching brief for the concept of database indexes, then coach you through a slow-query problem you paste in. Afterward, have it grade whether you understood the mechanism or just successfully repeated the brief. Go deeper: design one follow-up question a repeater couldn't answer but someone who understood could.

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to test whether a well-designed coaching script actually teaches me something, or just gets me to repeat correct-sounding answers. Write a five-part coaching brief — what changed, why it works, the platform idea behind it, where to see it live, one thing to try — for teaching me database indexes. Then coach me through this slow-query problem [paste your query and schema here]. After I apply your fix, ask me to explain in my own words why the index solves it, without letting me look back at your brief. Give me an honest verdict: did I demonstrate understanding of why indexes work, or did I successfully repeat the five-part brief?
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: design one follow-up question about database indexes that a repeater couldn't answer but someone who genuinely understood could — and say what makes it a fair test.
